You are the checking agent in an automated review of a short research report on a conjoint experiment. You receive the report, its result tables, the registration status of its analysis plan, and the issues raised by one or more automated reviewers. You do four things and return ONLY JSON.

1. Pressure-test claims. Find every quantitative or causal claim in the Abstract, Key findings and Results prose (at most 12, the most consequential first). For each, check it against the tables: the number, its sign, its interval, the outcome it is about, and whether the wording (e.g. "improved", "the only arm", "no effect") is justified. Verdicts: "supported", "overstated" (true number, too-strong wording or wrong scope), "unsupported" (number or direction not in the tables).
2. Give every reviewer issue a disposition:
   - "address": a different or additional estimate on the same data would answer it (covariates, estimator, weights, sample, a robustness re-fit);
   - "editorial": only prose, labels, tables or missing detail need fixing;
   - "declined": answering it would change the pre-registered analysis (for example, a multiple-testing correction the plan does not specify, a different primary outcome). Say which part of the plan it conflicts with. Registered analyses are never changed to satisfy a reviewer;
   - "unresolved": the data cannot settle it (needs a new sample, a different design, a measure that was not collected), or reviewers disagree in a way the tables cannot resolve.
3. Corrections: at most 6, and ONLY to fix a reported number, sign, interval, significance statement or plan status (registered, deviation, exploratory). This is a Light Pass: no corrections about style, framing, interpretation, design or methods. Address the writing agent, never "the authors": no person revises this report.
4. Unresolved questions: return an empty list (a Light Pass only verifies estimates and plan statuses).

Return:
{"assessment": "3-4 sentences: what the evidence supports, what it does not, and the single most important caveat",
 "claims": [{"claim": "short quote", "location": "Abstract|Key findings|H1|...", "verdict": "supported|overstated|unsupported", "evidence": "table and row, with the number", "fix": "rewording if not supported, else empty"}],
 "dispositions": [{"id": "R1", "disposition": "address|editorial|declined|unresolved", "reason": "one sentence"}],

## Registration

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-07 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint experiment*

<!-- fd:badges -->
![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: unreviewed](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #132,508](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: conjoint](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-07; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) raised sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
- Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.
- Among measured sharer attributes, close ties raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
- Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


Respondents were a YouGov sample of US adults, and the analysis used all 12,000 raw profile ratings, with none dropped for missing values on the main outcomes. Each profile attributed a headline to one of the respondent's real contacts. Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact were randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are measured attributes of those contacts, so their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes, not causal effects. True/neutral headlines are the reference level for information type (3,854 misinformation and 3,972 fact-check profiles were eligible). Standard errors are clustered by respondent, and tests are two-sided.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->
## Results

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Information type had large effects on sharing. Misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Chosen shares were 60.3% for true/neutral, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. These are causal contrasts, because headline type was randomized.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H2 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H2. Tie strength → sharing

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p = 0.003). This is a descriptive contrast on a measured attribute.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Continental US origin was 0.2 points above foreign origin (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p = 0.81). This is not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

A moderate sharer was chosen 1.9 points less often than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p = 0.034), a small difference close to the threshold. Conservative sharers were not distinguishable from liberal ones (−0.7 points, 95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]).

### H5. Trust in sharer → sharing

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

High trust in the sharer raised sharing by 5.7 points over low trust (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p < 0.001). Mid trust was 3.6 points higher, with an interval that includes zero (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3]).

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on sharing: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*

*AMCE of information type on plausibility: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was rated more plausible 18.6 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p < 0.001), and fact-checks 12.4 points less often (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2], p < 0.001). The pattern closely mirrors sharing.

messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished conjoint experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures. Write "p < 0.001" for any p-value below 0.001, never "p = 0.000".

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

Return ONLY JSON:
{"takeaways": [str, ...], "abstract": str, "design_notes": str, "results": {"H1": str, "H2": str, "S1": str, ...}, "exploratory": {"E1": str, ...}, "limitations": str}

## Literature note
The retrieved list is thin and mostly off-topic, so it says little directly about the hypotheses on source cues (tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge, conspiracy belief) and information type in sharing and plausibility. The closest items are general. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) discuss how misinformation spreads and influences people, and Roozenbeek et al. (2020) report predictors of belief in COVID-19 misinformation across countries, including links to health behaviours. Neither tests how sharer attributes shape sharing or plausibility, so neither bears on the AMCE estimates for H1-H14 or the weighted robustness checks R1-R12. Van Bavel et al. (2020) is a broad pandemic-response review with no abstract available. Three retrieved works are unrelated to the hypotheses: Dwivedi et al. (2019) on AI, Jenkins and Purushotma (2006) on media education, and Kniffin et al. (2020) on workplaces. The EMNLP 2021 proceedings entry (2021) is also unrelated. The works tagged as method concern attitudes toward the unvaccinated (Bor et al., 2022), election-lie acceptance (Arceneaux & Truex, 2022), and a vaccine-hesitancy survey with embedded conjoint experiments (Stamm et al., 2022). Only the last is a design precedent, as another conjoint on a health topic, and its abstract snippet reports no findings relevant here.

The retrieved works do not clearly disagree with each other or with the study's expectations, because none reports findings on the specific source-cue effects. The one tension is loose. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) frame misinformation as a broad societal problem, while Roozenbeek et al. (2020) locate susceptibility in individual and country-level predictors. Neither speaks to whether sharing depends on who shares, or to sharing without believing (X4). The study's conjoint design, which randomizes source attributes and measures both sharing and plausibility, can speak to that question directly, but the retrieved literature offers no benchmark against which to compare the estimates.

## This is a conjoint design
Each hypothesis with arms is one profile feature: the "arms" are its levels and the "control" is its reference level, so each
estimate is an AMCE (the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when the feature takes that level instead of the
reference, averaging over the other features). Write "levels" and "reference level", not "arms" and "control group".
Subgroup tables with columns mm_<group> and difference are differences in marginal means (the share of profiles with that
level that were chosen) between two respondent groups; name the levels whose difference is distinguishable from zero.
design.features marks each feature randomized true/false. Only randomized features have causal AMCEs; for the others say
once, plainly, that they are measured attributes whose AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes, and
never call them randomized. The abstract and takeaways must cover the whole design, not only its largest effect: give the
randomized feature's effects one sentence, then the measured features that matter and the registered subgroup differences
that are distinguishable from zero. Large, expected main effects are not the news when the design was built to study the
other features.

## Hypotheses and subgroups tagged exploratory (ids like X1, XS1)
These were specified by the authors after seeing the data and are estimated by the same deterministic scripts as the
registered tests (not by model-written code). Write a results[<id>] note for each, as for the registered ones, and say once
that they are post hoc. They may appear in at most two takeaways, each introduced as exploratory, and must never qualify a
registered result in the abstract. The pipeline's own exploratory analyses (E1, E2, ...) remain unreviewed model code.

## Abstract

Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings collected; models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer relative to low trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
- Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.
- Among measured sharer attributes, close ties were associated with 3.0 points more sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust with 5.7 points more (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
- Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


Respondents were a YouGov sample of US adults. Of 12,000 raw profile ratings, the models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility. Each profile attributed a headline to one of the respondent's real contacts. Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact were randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are measured attributes of those contacts, so their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes, not causal effects. True/neutral headlines are the reference level for information type (3,822 misinformation and 3,915 fact-check profiles in the sharing model). Standard errors are clustered by respondent, and tests are two-sided.

### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Information type had large effects on sharing. Misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Chosen shares were 60.3% for true/neutral, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. These are causal contrasts, because headline type was randomized.

OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings collected; models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer relative to low trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
- Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.
- Among measured sharer attributes, close ties were associated with 3.0 points more sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust with 5.7 points more (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
- Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


Respondents were a YouGov sample of US adults. Of 12,000 raw profile ratings, the models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility. Each profile attributed a headline to one of the respondent's real contacts. Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact were randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are measured attributes of those contacts, so their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes, not causal effects. True/neutral headlines are the reference level for information type (3,822 misinformation and 3,915 fact-check profiles in the sharing model). Standard errors are clustered by respondent, and tests are two-sided.

You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Randomize the sharer's attributes, with a behavioural share
Question: Does a sharer's tie strength or trust causally change willingness to share a false headline?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the design cause: randomizing attributes in vignettes turns the descriptive close-tie and high-trust contrasts into causal estimates and removes bundling with the real contact.
Design sketch: Crossed vignette: headline type (true, false, fact-check) x randomized sharer tie (close/distant) x randomized trust (high/low) shown as a forwarded post. The outcome is a real share to a mock feed, plus plausibility. Include a within-respondent block with each respondent's real contact as a benchmark. Sample is a YouGov-type US panel, with respondent clustering handled in the analysis.
Power target: about 2000 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (H2 close tie 0.030 vs MDE 0.0258; H5 high trust 0.057 vs MDE 0.051); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings collected; models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer relative to low trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.

Key findings:
- In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
- Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.
- Among measured sharer attributes, close ties were associated with 3.0 points more sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust with 5.7 points more (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
- Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.

Limitations: Many tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so the smaller effects (moderate sharer, close tie on plausibility, several subgroup contrasts) may be chance findings. Only headline type was randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are respondents' ratings of real contacts, so those AMCEs bundle correlated attributes and are not causal. Non-significant results are inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Health-topic and other subgroups are small. The exploratory X and XS analyses were specified after seeing the data and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

value.title: Randomize the sharer's attributes, with a behavioural share
value.rationale: In the source study close ties (+3.0 points, CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust (+5.7 points, CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, but these attributes were respondents' ratings of real contacts and so bundle correlated traits. Randomizing tie and trust in a forwarded-post vignette tests whether they cause sharing of false headlines (misinformation was shared 18.2 points less than true headlines).
value.contribution: Turns descriptive tie-strength and trust contrasts into causal estimates, using a behavioural share outcome and a real-contact benchmark.
limitations: Vignette sharers are fictional, so the effects may differ from those for real contacts.
The mock-feed share is a behavioural proxy and not a real platform share.
The 2000 per arm target is for a 0.03 effect, so smaller interaction effects will be underpowered.

design.title: Randomized sharer tie and trust in forwarded posts
design.overview: Respondents consent, then see forwarded posts. Headline type (true, false, fact-check) is randomized between respondents. Within each respondent, tie strength (close or distant) and trust (high or low) are randomized across two forwarded-post vignettes. Respondents choose whether to share each post to a mock feed and rate its plausibility. A final block shows a post attributed to the respondent's own real contact as a benchmark.
design.hypothesis: H1: a randomized close tie raises the probability of sharing by about 0.03. H2: randomized high trust raises it by about 0.05. Both effects hold for false headlines.
design.primaryOutcome: Share of the forwarded post to the mock feed (binary).
design.comparison: Close vs distant tie and high vs low trust, within headline type. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. Headline type is a between-subject factor.
design.population: US adults from a YouGov-type online panel.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. Type: generalizability_conditional (survey_experiment). Title: Does the misinformation penalty hold across belief in disputed claims?
Question: Is the gap in sharing misinformation vs true content smaller among respondents high in belief in disputed claims, and does the pattern hold in Spanish-language samples?

Estimate the infotype x moderator interaction with respondent-clustered SEs. Pre-register a single primary interaction.

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings collected; models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer relative to low trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.

Key findings:
- In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
- Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.
- Among measured sharer attributes, close ties were associated with 3.0 points more sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust with 5.7 points more (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
- Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.

Limitations: Many tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so the smaller effects (moderate sharer, close tie on plausibility, several subgroup contrasts) may be chance findings. Only headline type was randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are respondents' ratings of real contacts, so those AMCEs bundle correlated attributes and are not causal. Non-significant results are inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Health-topic and other subgroups are small. The exploratory X and XS analyses were specified after seeing the data and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

- Fix the H8 wording.
- Report the model Ns of 11,882 (share) and 11,884 (plausibility).
- Correct the eligible profile counts in the Design section.
- Describe the tie, trust and other source-attribute contrasts as associations, not effects that 'raised' sharing.
- State that the weighted moderate-sharer effect on sharing is not significant.

## Extensions already written (make yours distinct)
- mechanism: Randomize the sharer's attributes, with a behavioural share — H1: a randomized close tie raises the probability of sharing by about 0.03. H2: randomized high trust raises it by about 0.05. Both effects hold for false headlines.

value.title: Does the misinformation penalty hold across belief in disputed claims?
value.rationale: The source found misinformation shared 18.2 points less than true/neutral content (95% CI [-20.4,-16.0]), but respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more (p<0.001), a tertile contrast that was underpowered and US-English only. This design pre-selects belief in disputed claims as the moderator, stratifies on it and on survey language (English/Spanish), and tests one registered interaction.
value.contribution: Tests whether the misinformation sharing penalty shrinks among high-belief respondents and whether it generalizes to Spanish-language samples.
limitations: Interaction power is lower than main-effect power; language subgroup effects are exploratory.
Belief tertiles are measured, not randomized, so the moderator may bundle correlated traits.
Single-headline sharing intent differs from the source forced-choice pair design.

design.title: Headline type by belief in disputed claims and survey language
design.overview: Respondents first complete a belief-in-disputed-claims scale. They are then randomized to see a true/neutral or a false headline, and report sharing intent and plausibility. Recruitment is stratified by belief tertile and by language (English or Spanish).
design.hypothesis: The gap in sharing between misinformation and true/neutral headlines is smaller among respondents in the top tertile of belief in disputed claims than in the bottom tertile (a positive infotype-by-moderator interaction). The penalty is present in both languages.
design.primaryOutcome: Share: chosen/likely to share the headline (infotype x belief tertile interaction).
design.comparison: Misinformation vs true/neutral headline, interacted with belief tertile (top vs bottom), with respondent-clustered SEs; language is a secondary stratum.
design.population: Adults in the US, recruited via online panel, in English and Spanish, with quotas by belief tertile.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (data_collection). Title: No debate visible in the retrieved works
Question: Not applicable: the retrieved works do not frame a live disagreement that this design can discriminate.
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: The retrieved literature (COVID, AI, media education) does not bear directly on sharing from ties, so I decline to invent a debate. Instead this brief tests the measurement cause: whether sharing and plausibility are distinct.
Design sketch: Within-respondent design that measures plausibility, then sharing, in separate counterbalanced blocks, and adds a manipulation of accuracy salience (accuracy prompt vs none). If the misinformation sharing gap closes under the prompt while plausibility stays fixed, the two are separable. Use the same headline pool and a US panel.
Power target: about 1600 per arm to detect 0.031 at 80% power (H1 MDE 0.031; observed misinformation effect −0.182 leaves ample margin for detecting a partial reduction); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings collected; models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer relative to low trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.

Key findings:
- In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
- Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.
- Among measured sharer attributes, close ties were associated with 3.0 points more sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust with 5.7 points more (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
- Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.

Limitations: Many tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so the smaller effects (moderate sharer, close tie on plausibility, several subgroup contrasts) may be chance findings. Only headline type was randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are respondents' ratings of real contacts, so those AMCEs bundle correlated attributes and are not causal. Non-significant results are inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Health-topic and other subgroups are small. The exploratory X and XS analyses were specified after seeing the data and should be read as hypothesis-generating.
